group.title: Exact and rare
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Lasting only a very short time.
examples: The beauty of the cherry blossom is {ephemeral}.
wrong: The ephemeral monument will stand for a thousand years.

words.meaning: To make a bad situation better.
examples: New laws were passed to {ameliorate} working conditions.
wrong: The storm ameliorated the damage by making the roof collapse.

words.meaning: Appearing to be true, but perhaps not really so.
examples: The {ostensible} reason for the visit was business.
wrong: The ostensible reason was the real one, which everybody had confirmed.

words.meaning: To make a problem worse.
examples: Shouting will only {exacerbate} the situation.
wrong: The cool rain exacerbated the fire by putting it out.

words.meaning: To make a process happen more quickly.
examples: Extra staff will {expedite} the visa process.
wrong: More forms will expedite the process by delaying it for months.

words.meaning: To increase quickly in number.
examples: Small cafés {proliferate} in the old part of the city.
wrong: The rare birds proliferated until only two were left.

words.meaning: To place different things next to each other for contrast.
examples: The exhibition will {juxtapose} old and new photographs.
wrong: She juxtaposed the two photographs by throwing one away.

words.meaning: To make something unclear or hard to understand.
examples: The report seems to {obfuscate} the real costs.
wrong: The teacher obfuscated the lesson by explaining it simply and clearly.

words.meaning: Showing wealth in a way meant to impress.
examples: He lived in an {ostentatious} mansion with gold gates.
wrong: She wore a plain, modest dress at the party, which was very ostentatious.

words.meaning: Very unwilling to spend money.
examples: The {parsimonious} owner refused to buy new chairs.
wrong: He is parsimonious, so he spends money freely on every luxury.

words.meaning: Very weak or slight.
examples: The link between the two events is {tenuous}.
wrong: The tenuous rope was thick enough to hold a ship.

words.meaning: Clear and without any doubt.
examples: She gave an {unequivocal} answer: no.
wrong: His unequivocal reply left everyone unsure of what he meant.

words.meaning: To show that someone was right after being blamed.
examples: The new evidence will {vindicate} the engineer.
wrong: The new evidence vindicated the claim by proving it was false.

words.meaning: Open to more than one meaning, often to avoid giving a clear answer.
examples: His {equivocal} reply told us nothing.
wrong: She gave an equivocal answer by saying a plain, definite yes.

words.meaning: Very careful about details and cleanliness.
examples: He is {fastidious} about how his desk looks.
wrong: A fastidious cook leaves the kitchen dirty and does not care.

words.meaning: Done without a good reason and often harmful.
examples: The film has too much {gratuitous} violence.
wrong: The gratuitous gift was a necessary payment that the law required.

words.meaning: A force that makes something start or move faster.
examples: The scandal gave {impetus} to the reform.
wrong: The impetus stopped the project from ever beginning.

words.meaning: Harmful in a gradual way that is hard to notice.
examples: The disease is {insidious}; symptoms appear late.
wrong: An insidious danger is one that is loud and obvious to everyone at once.

words.meaning: Clear and easy to understand.
examples: She gave a {lucid} explanation of the theory.
wrong: His lucid writing was so confusing that nobody could follow it.

words.meaning: Easy to shape or influence.
examples: Gold is a {malleable} metal.
wrong: A malleable metal is one so hard that it cannot be shaped at all.

words.meaning: Unclear and vague.
examples: The plan remained {nebulous}.
wrong: He gave a nebulous answer with every detail stated exactly.

words.meaning: Calm and not seeming worried.
examples: He was {nonchalant} about the exam.
wrong: She was nonchalant, so she shook with fear and cried.

words.meaning: Spreading through every part of something.
examples: A {pervasive} smell of smoke filled the house.
wrong: The pervasive smell was in one tiny corner only.

words.meaning: Being the perfect example of something.
examples: She is the {quintessential} teacher: patient and kind.
wrong: He is the quintessential athlete who can’t run and hates all sport.

words.meaning: Stubbornly refusing to obey.
examples: The {recalcitrant} student ignored every instruction.
wrong: The recalcitrant child obeyed every rule at once and gladly.

words.meaning: Very honest and careful to do the right thing.
examples: He is {scrupulous} about paying his taxes.
wrong: The scrupulous accountant cheated the company for years.

words.meaning: Understood without being said.
examples: There was a {tacit} agreement not to mention the accident.
wrong: They shouted the tacit agreement aloud in front of everyone.

words.meaning: A feeling of fear about something that may happen.
examples: She opened the letter with {trepidation}.
wrong: He walked into the party with trepidation, full of joy and no worry at all.

words.meaning: Showing strong feeling.
examples: He made a {vehement} protest against the plan.
wrong: His vehement reply was calm, soft and without any feeling.

words.meaning: Playful and unusual in a charming way.
examples: The garden has a {whimsical} collection of statues.
wrong: The whimsical design was strict, serious and completely ordinary.

words.meaning: Full of eager energy for a cause.
examples: The {zealous} volunteers worked all night.
wrong: The zealous worker did the minimum and left early with no interest.

words.meaning: To agree to something without arguing, often reluctantly.
examples: After a long talk, she decided to {acquiesce}.
wrong: He acquiesced by arguing loudly against the idea and refusing to move.

words.meaning: To give a false idea of something.
examples: His calm voice {belies} how worried he is.
wrong: His clear voice belied nothing, since it matched what he really felt exactly.

words.meaning: Clear, logical and convincing.
examples: She made a {cogent} argument for change.
wrong: His cogent argument was so illogical that it convinced nobody.

words.meaning: Able to speak or write in a clear, convincing way.
examples: She gave an {eloquent} speech.
wrong: An eloquent speaker mumbles and cannot find a single word.

words.meaning: Treating all sides fairly.
examples: A judge must be {impartial}.
wrong: The impartial judge always took the side of her friend.

words.meaning: Strange because it does not fit with its surroundings.
examples: A neon sign looked {incongruous} on the old church.
wrong: The incongruous painting matched the room perfectly in every way.

words.meaning: Too great to be put into words.
examples: The view filled her with {ineffable} joy.
wrong: The ineffable feeling was easy to describe in one short word.

words.meaning: Using very few words.
examples: His {laconic} reply was just one word: no.
wrong: The laconic speaker gave a long speech and used hundreds of words.

words.meaning: Having mixed feelings about something.
examples: She felt {ambivalent} about moving abroad.
wrong: He felt ambivalent because he was completely sure and had no doubts.
